# Implementation

:::

In earlier chapters of this course, a comprehensive introduction was provided regarding handling data, feeding it into models, and evaluating the performance. However, when working with healthcare data, data collection is complicated. In the data sources and data acquisition module, a range of data providers was introduced along with the notions of privacy and data protection. These concepts are beyond the scope of this course, but it is important that the sensitive nature of these databases is understood, which is why the data are safeguarded by some major data holders. This has the positive effect, besides securing the privacy of individuals, that certain standards can be implemented by these data holders. A standard for interacting with databases is the FHIR standard. This standard streamlines how healthcare data is interacted with globally.

The FHIR standard often uses Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) for data exchange. Such systems use servers and networks. Thus, an understanding of these components is essential. Furthermore, an understanding of the FHIR standard itself is also important when healthcare data is used for dynamic risk prediction. Therefore, in this section of the course, the following will be addressed:

- Hosting and access to data
- FHIR
- Validation
- **Exercises**

# Hosting and access to data
When models for dynamic risk prediction are built, multiple actors are involved, and particularly in the healthcare sector, interaction with partners is certain.
These partners are the personnel who collect and safeguard the data. Clinicians who collect data cannot safeguard it on their own. The data must be stored in a location that is easily accessible, secure, and allows for the storage of all data from every clinician at a regional, national, or international level. This makes [servers](https://medium.com/@theoluwafemi/understanding-servers-cbc61f910b9b) a major part of the digital infrastructure. Through this infrastructure, information about patients, diagnoses, treatments, etc., can be transferred and stored by researchers. By these components, the provision of the best service, the conduct of research, and the support of decision-making processes are facilitated.

A server is a type of computer by which data are hosted or a service is provided to other computers via a [network](https://medium.com/@Mushtaque1503/what-is-computer-network-and-types-of-network-and-how-does-it-work-55cbe160245b).
Communication and sharing of resources or information are enabled between two or more computers when a network is utilized. Network types are classified from local, such as Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, to wider area networks, including university systems or the internet. Resources, such as databases concerning the Danish population, are primarily accessed via these broader networks.

These networks are composed of physical devices (hardware), such as routers or access points, which enable data retrieval and transmission to intended locations within the networks. Through these mechanisms, the sharing of resources is facilitated, and the distribution of information is secured within seconds.

The term 'server' refers to the physical or virtual computer itself, or more broadly, to the system including the computer and its operating system. Servers typically operate within a client-server architecture, a fundamental model of network interaction. The client-to-server connection can be illustrated as follows:

<div style="text-align: left;">
  <img src="../images/implementation/server_to_client.png" alt="Image" style="margin-bottom: 15px; width: min(700px, 100%);">
</div>

Servers are composed of both hardware, typically located in a server room, and software, through which services are provided to those with server access. Multiple servers for different purposes and functionalities can be hosted within a single physical server.

Different types of servers, such as those for websites, search engines, and email services, are utilized daily. In the case of dynamic risk prediction are servers that contain important databases. An introduction to databases was introduced in the data management section.

A database server is a type of server through which information is managed for easy access, management, and updating. A single database server can host multiple databases. These types of servers can be linked to other servers where predictive models are hosted. By this method, data are kept near the database, and the risk of accidental data leakage is minimized. Easy and secure interaction between data, models, and the user interface is facilitated by this network of servers.

This process can be seen in the figure below.

<div style="text-align: left;">
  <img src="../images/implementation/imp_overlook.png" alt="Image" style="margin-bottom: 15px; width: min(700px, 100%);">
</div>

In the figure, the data management component and the making of the predictive model that is hosted on the server are shown as responsibilities directly held by the researcher.
Access to data is typically not direct, it is an [Application Programming Interface (APIs)](https://medium.com/@vinayak-singh/what-is-an-api-its-types-and-protocols-used-bfaad3fa8e77), which are generally involved, acting as a bridge between the user and the databases.
This approach is effective because it allows for the establishment of automated, scheduled tasks (Via CronJobs) and can overcome restrictive database access.
For example, such jobs could involve weather projections being retrieved daily at midnight for display on an app or webpage.

More case-based API usages also exist, such as when a transaction is completed using third-party systems (like [Apple Pay](https://www.apple.com/apple-pay/)), or when the current temperature (not just the projected one) is displayed by a weather app.

For each API, a set of rules and techniques is established that outlines how the API should be implemented and used.
These rules and techniques are known as the API protocol, and by them, applicable data formats and commands are determined.
Many different API protocols exist, but the [Representational State Transfer (REST) protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REST) is particularly relevant to this course.
REST is considered versatile, as no single message format is enforced by the style itself for the messages that can be handled.
For REST interactions, a URL is used as the endpoint, and HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PATCH, PUT, and DELETE) are employed to perform operations such as resource creation, reading, updating, and deletion (CRUD). The relevance of this protocol is established by its facilitation of interactions that enable data exchange between servers and clients. An API that adheres to this protocol is referred to as a RESTful API or, simply a REST API.

An example of a standard that leverages the principles of the RESTful API and is widely utilized in the healthcare sector is FHIR.

# FHIR
[Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)](https://www.healthit.gov/topic/standards-technology/standards/fhir) is a global health care reporting standard and interface published by HL7 designed to facilitate the exchange of health data.
It supports the RESTful architecture, such that [all systems can read all resources](https://www.hl7.org/fhir/summary.html), which is particularly important, as it can potentially support omics data (data with an -omics ending, such as genomics).
Additionally, it is user-friendly in the sense that all resources have a readable text representation in addition to the computer-readable text.
It gives the user the ability to build live applications in collaboration with other researchers.

Regarding Danish health data, FHIR has already enabled [systems for electronic patient records at the hospitals and municipalities (Columna CIS and Columna Cura), along with other Danish applications and systems](https://hl7.dk/FHIR-implementations-1.0.0.html).
The list of implemented systems will most likely continue to grow, as more projects are using FHIR.

The usage of FHIR in the research process can be seen below as a way to access the live data and thus feed the predictive model.

<div style="text-align: left;">
  <img src="../images/implementation/imp_overlook_fhir.png" alt="Image" style="margin-bottom: 15px; width: min(700px, 100%);">
</div>

The FHIR [administration module](https://www.hl7.org/fhir/administration-module.html) covers most of the basic live data relevant to medical research, and the remaining info can be obtained using various other FHIR modules.
Considering the **motivational example** from the introduction of the course, relevant live data would be:

- Patient: the baseline information about the person (e.g., name and age), along with something unique to identify them by (e.g., CPR number in Denmark).
- EpisodeOfCare: Information about long-term care episodes, along with diagnoses and a time frame of when they were in care.
- Encounter: Short-term care, or contact with health care providers.
- Observation: Anything measured, such as weight, the results of any blood tests, or the like.
- Procedure: Drug administrations, surgeries, and various tests such as X-rays.

The first three points are from the administration module, the fourth point is from the [diagnostic module](https://www.hl7.org/fhir/diagnostics-module.html), and the final point is from the [clinical module](https://www.hl7.org/fhir/clinicalsummary-module.html).

Similar to the model validation discussed previously, the validation of the model's implementation is also of importance.

# Validation
In terms of implementation validation, there are [three main types](https://www.learngxp.com/good-validation-practices/the-difference-between-prospective-concurrent-and-retrospective-validation/): prospective, concurrent, and retrospective.

The prospective validation is arguably the most important one, as it validates that the system performs as intended, based on its protocols, *before* the system is used in practice.
The validation process checks not just if the predictive model is accurate, but also whether the implementation of it is made correctly.
The validation process typically follows a systematic approach, starting with the process design, then going through the installation, operational, and performance qualifications.
It is typically required that the system pass the validation checks before it is deployed.

Next is the concurrent validation, which is relevant when the system has been implemented and used.
It serves to check whether the system is still in control and compliant.
This type of validation is typically used when something related to the system is changed, such as the introduction of new data (e.g., another hospital's data is made available and is used in the model), a change of equipment, or something else.
As it is concurrent, any deviations found can be corrected on an ongoing basis.

Finally, consider the retrospective validation, which uses historical data and records to validate the system.
The main reason to use this type of validation is if no prospective validation was made before launch, and thus, no evidence for the system's efficiency exists.

This section has provided a basic understanding of how the digital healthcare infrastructure works in terms of exchanging data, relevant for secure access in the context of dynamic risk prediction. Where the the importance of servers and networks in hosting sensitive patient information to the standardization brought by APIs and specifically the FHIR standard have been addressed. Also, the importance of validation processes—prospective, and retrospective—ensures the reliability and compliance of implemented systems. These components are essential in the process of building accurate predictive models and maintaining data security.
